newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines orders new bidding for container port.
newsitem.headline: Philippines orders new bidding for container port.

text.p: Philippines President Fidel Ramos on Thursday cancelled bidding for a container port terminal at Subic Bay, one of the country's largest privatisation projects, and ordered the process be started anew.

He also ordered the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) not to enter into a contract with Hutchison Ports Philippines Limited, a unit of Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa, which had been recommended by the SBMA after bidding last year.

"We have found the terms of reference provided in the tender document to have been disregarded by the SBMA Bids and Awards Committee in its determination of the winning bid," Ramos said in a letter to SBMA chairman Richard Gordon, copies of which were distributed.
"Accordingly you are ordered to refrain from signing the contract with Hutchison Ports Philippines Limited," the letter said.
"You are instructed to conduct a re-bidding for the same, giving all interested parties the opportunity to qualify and participate in the re-bid," Ramos said.
The Subic project became controversial when Philippine port operator International Container Terminal Services (ICTSI) protested after being edged out in the bidding.
Ramos then ordered a review of the process.

SBMA rejected ICTSI's original bid on the grounds that it would violate a law forbidding monopolies in the port industry. ICTSI operates the Manila International Container Terminal, which handles 70 percent of container traffic in the country.

It said it also rejected ICTSI's contention that the only financial factor to be looked into was royalty per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU). In the original bidding in August, ICTSI gave the highest royalty of $58 per TEU, followed by Hutchison with $20.50 and Germany's Royal Port Services with $15.00.
But Hutchison had promised to build more wharfs at Subic in the fourth year of the 25-year contract, as compared to the ninth year proposed by ICTSI.
Neither ICTSI nor Hutchison were immediately available for comment.
But businessmen and analysts said the terms of reference at the re-bidding would have to be made clear.
"The criteria for the re-bidding should be transparent and all issues should be discussed with prospective bidders so there will be clear understanding," said industrialist Raul Concepcion.

"Hutchison will be harping on the reversal of the decision," said Joel Mendoza, research head at Urbancorp Securities. "It may affect investor confidence in the government's awarding of contracts unless it is properly explained."

"If you change decisions already made, and there have been many times when this has happened, it puts into question whether the government has firm policies .. the permanence of stability in its decisions," said political analyst Amando Doronila. "It will weaken or undermine confidence in our business procedures."
Government officials however defended the decision.
"Under the circumstances, a re-bid is the fairest, most acceptable (and legally defensible) solution to the current impasse," Executive Secretary Ruben Torres said in a statement.
